lead: Cloud work is done by named actors, not by an unnamed 'cloud'. A consumer buys a service; a provider owns the shared pool; a broker aggregates and resells; an auditor checks logs and compliance independently; a carrier supplies the network link. Around them sit boundaries: who legally owns the data, who can see or change it, and who manages which layer. Under them sits a meter that turns usage into money. These roles, boundaries and the bill decide what a cloud service really is.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for cost risks, Chapter 1.5 for the actor view, and Chapter 1.6 for the responsibility boundary.

blocks.text: Every cloud transaction has at least two actors. The consumer uses the service and pays for it. The provider owns and operates the physical pool: servers, disks, switches and the software that divides them. A broker sits between many providers and one consumer; it aggregates catalogues and resells, often adding a portal or a billing layer. An auditor checks the provider independently: logs, controls and compliance evidence, without running the service. A carrier supplies the connection from the consumer's network to the provider's edge; it does not own the compute pool. The broker and auditor are the two roles most often left out of answers. The figure shows the five actors and the direction of each relationship. The same person can be consumer and provider in a private cloud, but the roles stay separate in an answer because each carries different duties.

An organisational boundary marks who legally owns the data and who is accountable for it. Moving data to a provider does not transfer ownership; a regulator or a customer still looks to the consumer. A trust boundary marks what one party can see and change. The provider's staff may operate the hypervisor but should not read the consumer's files; encryption and access control draw this line. The responsibility boundary is the cut from chapter 1.6: below it the provider patches and monitors, above it the consumer patches and monitors. In IaaS the cut is low; in SaaS it is high. These boundaries are different questions. A data set can be legally owned by the consumer, inside the provider's trust boundary, while the provider manages the storage layer. An answer that says 'the cloud provider is responsible for security' has collapsed all three boundaries into one.

Cloud spending changes shape. Capital expense (capex) is money spent before use: buying servers, racks and cooling. Operating expense (opex) is money spent as the service runs: hourly compute, storage and requests. Cloud moves capex to opex, which helps cash flow but can raise the total if use is steady for years. Economies of scale mean a large provider buys hardware, power and staff more cheaply per unit than a small team can; part of that saving is passed to the consumer. Metering makes pay-per-use possible. Common meters are per second or per hour of a virtual machine, per GB-month of storage, and per million requests or API calls. On-demand pricing has no commitment and follows the meter. Reserved pricing asks for a one- or three-year commitment in return for a discount; it suits a base load that will not disappear. Total cost of ownership (TCO) adds everything: the bill, staff time, migration, training, network egress and the cost of leaving. Price is only the provider's line on the bill; cost is the whole owner's ledger. An SLA is the contract that names the service, its measurable targets and the penalties. An SLO is one target inside it. For example, 99.9% availability in a 30-day month allows at most 43 minutes of downtime.

blocks.where: D is allowed downtime, A is the availability target as a fraction, and T is the period in the same time unit. With A = 0.999 and T = 43,200 minutes (30 days), D = 43.2 minutes.

items: Compute: virtual machines or containers, billed by time.
Storage: object buckets or block volumes, billed by GB-month.
Managed database: the provider runs the engine, billed by instance and storage.
OpenStack: open-source private-pool stack with compute, object storage and networking.

figure.caption: The consumer buys from the provider; the broker resells to the consumer, the auditor checks the provider independently, and the carrier supplies the network link. Notice that the broker and auditor are separate from the provider.

spec.aria: Five actors drawn as a graph: the consumer buys from the provider, the broker resells to the consumer, the auditor checks the provider, and the carrier supplies the network link.

examples.question: A team runs 4 virtual machines at ₹6 per VM-hour, 24 hours a day, through a 30-day month. It keeps 500 GB of storage at ₹2 per GB per month and serves 20 million requests at ₹0.5 per million requests. (a) Find the on-demand monthly bill. (b) A one-year reserved contract takes 40% off compute; find the new bill and the monthly and yearly saving.
steps: Compute hours = 4 VMs × 24 hours/day × 30 days = 2,880 VM-hours.
examples.answer: On-demand bill ₹18,290 per month; one-year reserved bill ₹11,378 per month; saving ₹6,912 per month or ₹82,944 per year for the same 4 virtual machines.
examples.check:
vm_hours = 4 * 24 * 30
compute = vm_hours * 6
storage = 500 * 2
requests = int(20 * 0.5)
total = compute + storage + requests
reserved_compute = int(compute * 0.6)
reserved_total = reserved_compute + storage + requests
saving_month = total - reserved_total
saving_year = saving_month * 12
for x in [vm_hours, compute, storage, requests, total, reserved_compute, reserved_total, saving_month, saving_year]:
    print(x)

traps: Leaving out the broker and auditor; most answers name only consumer and provider.
Swapping SLA and SLO: the SLA is the contract, the SLO is one target inside it.
Calling price cost: TCO includes staff time, migration, training, egress and exit.
Treating the organisational boundary as the trust boundary: legal ownership and technical visibility are different.
Assuming a reserved discount always lowers TCO: it helps only if the base load lasts for the commitment.

quiz.q: Name the five actor roles in the cloud actor view.
Why can one firm be both consumer and provider in a private cloud, yet the roles stay separate?
quiz.a: The firm buys and uses the service and also owns the pool, but the consumer role carries data ownership and the provider role carries operation of the shared hardware; an answer must name both duties.

quiz.q: A service runs 2 VMs at ₹5 per VM-hour for 24 hours a day for a 30-day month. Find the monthly compute charge.
A team has a steady load of 4 VMs all year. On-demand is ₹6 per VM-hour; a one-year reserved contract gives 40% off compute. Compare monthly cost and saving.
quiz.a: On-demand compute = 4 × 720 × 6 = ₹17,280. Reserved compute = 17,280 × 0.60 = ₹10,368. Saving = ₹6,912 per month.

quiz.q: State one difference between organisational boundary and trust boundary.
quiz.a: Organisational boundary is legal ownership and accountability for data; trust boundary is what one party can technically see and change.

quiz.q: An SLA promises 99.9% availability in a 30-day month. Find the allowed downtime in minutes.
Give two reasons a lower monthly cloud bill may still raise TCO.
quiz.a: Migration and staff training are one-time or ongoing costs outside the bill; network egress and exit charges can also rise. TCO adds these to the bill.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry calls the ongoing control of cloud spend FinOps; it watches unit cost, not only the monthly total. Reserved and spot pricing, egress charges and carbon-aware scheduling are active areas. Search for cloud unit economics, FinOps Foundation, spot instance interruption and cloud carbon footprint for the next layer.
